description: Audit and redesign your sleep environment and habits using sleep science: light exposure timing, temperature regulation, caffeine half-life, and consistent wake time. Sleep is the single highest-leverage health intervention.

steps.description: Measure your current sleep baseline for 7 days: time to bed, time to sleep, wake-ups, wake time, and subjective quality rating.

inputs.name: current-sleep-habits
inputs.desc: Your current sleep and wake times, bedroom environment, and pre-sleep routine

inputs.name: sleep-complaints
inputs.desc: What is wrong with your sleep: trouble falling asleep, waking up, not feeling rested, inconsistent schedule

outputs.name: sleep-baseline
outputs.desc: 7-day log: bedtime, estimated time to fall asleep, number of wake-ups, final wake time, total estimated sleep, and quality rating 1-10

outputs.name: sleep-patterns
outputs.desc: Patterns identified: weekend vs weekday differences, time-to-sleep trends, quality correlations

process: Track for 7 consecutive days using a simple log. Record: what time you got in bed, what time you estimate you fell asleep, how many times you woke up, what time you finally woke up, and rate the quality 1-10.

Calculate averages: average time to fall asleep (sleep latency), average total sleep time, average quality rating. Sleep latency over 20 minutes indicates a problem with your pre-sleep routine or timing.
Note the weekend-weekday difference. If you sleep 2+ hours more on weekends, you are carrying sleep debt. The weekend is not 'catching up'; it is evidence that weeknight sleep is insufficient.
Identify the biggest lever: is the problem falling asleep (latency), staying asleep (wake-ups), or not sleeping long enough (early alarm)? Each has a different solution.

steps.description: Design your light exposure: bright light within 30 minutes of waking, dim light 2 hours before sleep, zero blue light in the last hour.

outputs.name: light-protocol
outputs.desc: Morning: 10+ minutes of bright outdoor light within 30 minutes of waking. Evening: dim warm light after sunset. Last hour: no screens or blue-blocking glasses.

outputs.name: environment-changes
outputs.desc: Physical changes to implement: blackout curtains, warm-spectrum evening bulbs, morning light alarm

process: Morning light exposure is the most important circadian signal. Get outside within 30 minutes of waking for 10+ minutes. Overcast days still provide 10x more lux than indoor lighting.
Evening light exposure is the most common sleep disruptor. After sunset, switch to warm-spectrum (below 3000K) bulbs. Standard LED bulbs emit blue wavelengths that suppress melatonin production.
In the last hour before bed, eliminate screens or use blue-blocking glasses. The evidence for blue-blocking glasses is moderate; the evidence for eliminating screens entirely is strong.
Blackout curtains are non-negotiable if your bedroom gets any outside light. Even small amounts of light through the eyelids disrupt deep sleep stages.

steps.description: Set bedroom temperature and sleep timing for optimal sleep quality.

outputs.name: temperature-protocol
outputs.desc: Bedroom temperature 65-68F (18-20C). A warm shower 90 minutes before bed triggers a core temperature drop that signals sleep onset.

outputs.name: sleep-timing
outputs.desc: Fixed wake time 7 days per week (not bedtime). The body's circadian clock anchors to wake time, not sleep time.

process: Set the bedroom to 65-68F (18-20C). Core body temperature must drop for sleep onset. A room that is too warm prevents this drop. Most people keep their bedrooms 5-10 degrees too warm.
A warm shower or bath 90 minutes before bed accelerates the core temperature drop. The warm water brings blood to the surface; when you step out, the rapid cooling triggers sleepiness.

Fix your wake time, not your bedtime. Wake up at the same time 7 days per week, including weekends. The circadian clock anchors to wake time. A variable bedtime is fine; a variable wake time disrupts the clock.
Caffeine has a 6-hour half-life. Coffee at 2pm means 50% of the caffeine is still active at 8pm. Set a caffeine cutoff time 8-10 hours before your target sleep time.

steps.description: Design a 30-minute wind-down routine that transitions your brain from active to sleep-ready.

outputs.name: wind-down-routine
outputs.desc: A specific 30-minute routine: what you do, in what order, starting at the same time each night

outputs.name: removal-list
outputs.desc: Activities to remove from the pre-sleep period: screens, work email, news, intense exercise, heavy meals

process: Start the routine at the same time each night, 30 minutes before target sleep time. Consistency trains the brain to associate the routine with sleep onset.
The routine should be low-stimulation: reading (paper, not screen), stretching, journaling, breathing exercises, or quiet conversation. Not TV, not social media, not work email.
If racing thoughts prevent sleep, use a 'worry journal': spend 5 minutes writing everything on your mind. The act of writing externalizes the thoughts and reduces their activation.

Do not exercise within 3 hours of sleep. Exercise raises core temperature and cortisol, both of which delay sleep onset. Morning or early afternoon exercise improves sleep quality; evening exercise disrupts it.

steps.description: Track improvements over 30 days and adjust: compare sleep latency, quality, and energy levels to your baseline.

outputs.name: improvement-data
outputs.desc: 30-day comparison: sleep latency (should decrease), quality rating (should increase), and daytime energy (should improve)

outputs.name: adjustments
outputs.desc: What to tweak: if latency is still high, the timing or routine needs adjustment. If quality is still low, the environment needs work.

process: Continue the sleep log for 30 days after implementing changes. Compare week 4 to the baseline.
Expected improvements: sleep latency drops below 15 minutes, quality rating increases by 2+ points, weekend-weekday gap shrinks.
If latency is still high after 2 weeks, adjust timing: try going to bed 30 minutes later. A shorter window of time in bed with better sleep is more restorative than a longer window with poor sleep.
If wake-ups persist, check the environment: room temperature, noise, light leaks. If the environment is clean, consider whether alcohol or late meals are contributing.

description: Manage energy, not time. Time management fails because it treats all hours as equal. Energy management recognizes that a focused hour produces more than three depleted hours. Map your energy cycles and schedule accordingly.

steps.description: Map your personal energy cycle: when are you sharpest, when do you fade, and what causes energy crashes.

inputs.name: energy-complaints
inputs.desc: When you feel most drained or unfocused

outputs.name: energy-map
outputs.desc: Hourly energy ratings for a typical day: morning, mid-morning, post-lunch, afternoon, evening. Rated 1-10.

outputs.name: crash-triggers
outputs.desc: Activities or times that reliably cause energy drops: meetings, meals, poor sleep, specific types of work

process: For 5 workdays, rate your energy 1-10 at each hour from waking to sleeping. Use a simple scale: 10 = sharp and focused, 5 = functional but not sharp, 1 = barely functioning.
Identify the pattern: most people have a peak in the morning (9-11am), a dip after lunch (1-3pm), and a secondary peak in late afternoon (4-6pm). Your pattern may differ.
Identify crash triggers: what reliably drops your energy? Long meetings, heavy lunches, poor sleep the night before, specific types of administrative work.
The energy map is your scheduling template. High-energy hours get the hardest work. Low-energy hours get routine tasks.

steps.description: Match your tasks to your energy level: deep work during peaks, routine work during troughs, creative work during the secondary peak.

outputs.name: optimized-schedule
outputs.desc: Your schedule reorganized by energy: deep work at peak, meetings and admin at trough, creative work at secondary peak

outputs.name: protected-blocks
outputs.desc: Time blocks that are protected from meetings and interruptions because they are your peak energy hours

process: Deep work (analysis, writing, coding, strategy) goes in your peak energy window. For most people, this is 9-11am. Never schedule a meeting during your peak.
Routine work (email, admin, scheduling, reporting) goes in your energy trough. For most people, this is 1-3pm. These tasks require less cognitive energy and are resilient to low focus.
Creative work (brainstorming, problem-solving, ideation) goes in the secondary peak. Some research suggests that slightly lower inhibition (moderate fatigue) actually helps creativity.
Protect the peak: block it on your calendar. No meetings, no email, no Slack. If you give away your peak hours to meetings, you are doing your hardest work during your worst hours.

steps.description: Design renewal rituals for the trough: movement, nutrition, social interaction, or nature exposure that restore energy without caffeine.

outputs.name: renewal-rituals
outputs.desc: Specific rituals for each energy trough: a 10-minute walk after lunch, a mid-afternoon stretching break, a conversation with a colleague

outputs.name: energy-sustaining-habits
outputs.desc: Daily habits that maintain energy: hydration schedule, meal timing, movement frequency

process: A 10-minute walk after lunch reduces the post-lunch energy dip significantly. The combination of movement and light exposure resets alertness.
Hydration affects energy more than most people realize. Mild dehydration (1-2% body weight) reduces cognitive performance by 10-20%. Drink water before you feel thirsty.

Small frequent meals sustain energy better than large infrequent ones. A heavy lunch causes a large insulin response and a corresponding energy crash. A lighter lunch with protein maintains afternoon energy.

Social interaction can be energizing or draining depending on the interaction. A brief positive conversation restores energy. A contentious meeting drains it. Schedule social interactions strategically.

steps.description: Track your energy for 30 days under the new system and iterate on the schedule.

outputs.name: energy-improvement
outputs.desc: Comparison of average daily energy before and after the system: should see higher peak energy and shorter/shallower troughs

outputs.name: schedule-refinements
outputs.desc: Adjustments based on what worked and what did not

process: Continue the hourly energy rating for 30 days. Compare week 4 to the original baseline.
Expected improvements: peak energy hours feel sharper (because they are now protected), trough hours feel less drained (because they have renewal rituals), and total productive output increases.

If peak hours are still being invaded by meetings, the protection is not working. Communicate boundaries explicitly: 'I am available for meetings after 11am. Before that, I am heads-down on project work.'
Iterate quarterly: energy cycles shift with seasons, life changes, and work demands. What worked in Q1 may not work in Q3.

description: Build new habits by stacking them onto existing ones. The existing habit is the trigger; the new habit is the response. No willpower required because the trigger is already automatic.

steps.description: List every automatic habit you already do daily: things you do without thinking, at the same time, in the same sequence.

inputs.name: target-habit
inputs.desc: The new habit you want to build

inputs.name: daily-routine
inputs.desc: Your current daily routine from waking to sleeping

outputs.name: habit-inventory
outputs.desc: Every automatic daily habit: brush teeth, make coffee, sit at desk, check phone, eat lunch, etc.

outputs.name: habit-timing
outputs.desc: When each automatic habit occurs and how long it takes

process: Walk through your day from waking to sleeping and write down every action that happens automatically: things you do without deciding to do them.
Focus on the transitions: waking up, arriving at work, finishing lunch, getting home. Transitions are natural stack points because they already have a trigger (the preceding event).
Note which habits are deeply ingrained (never skipped) versus loosely held (sometimes skipped). Only stack onto deeply ingrained habits.
The best stack points are habits that: happen daily, happen at a consistent time, require minimal effort, and are followed by a natural pause.

steps.description: Match your target habit to the best stack point: the existing habit that is most natural to pair it with.

outputs.name: stack-formula
outputs.desc: The specific formula: 'After I [existing habit], I will [new habit].' Example: 'After I pour my morning coffee, I will journal for 5 minutes.'

outputs.name: stack-compatibility
outputs.desc: Why this stack point works: same location, same energy level, natural transition, no conflicting activity

process: The stack formula is: 'After I [existing habit], I will [new habit].' The existing habit is the trigger. The new habit is the response.

Select the stack point based on compatibility: same physical location (stacking a kitchen habit onto a bedroom habit fails), appropriate energy level (stacking exercise onto the post-lunch slump fails), and no conflicting activity.

Make the new habit tiny: the initial version should take 2 minutes or less. 'After I pour coffee, I will meditate' fails if meditation means 20 minutes. 'After I pour coffee, I will take 3 deep breaths' succeeds because it takes 15 seconds.
The tiny version is not the final version. It is the entry point. Once the stack is automatic (2-3 weeks), you expand the duration incrementally.

steps.description: Prepare the physical environment so the new habit requires zero setup when the trigger fires.

outputs.name: environment-setup
outputs.desc: Physical changes that make the new habit frictionless: supplies laid out, space cleared, tools accessible

outputs.name: friction-removal
outputs.desc: Every obstacle between the trigger and the new habit, with a solution for each

process: The new habit must require zero decisions when the trigger fires. If the trigger is 'after I pour coffee' and the habit is 'journal for 5 minutes,' the journal and pen must be next to the coffee maker.

Remove every friction point: if the journal is in a drawer, you will skip it. If the pen is dead, you will skip it. If the table is cluttered, you will skip it. Make the habit the path of least resistance.
Add friction to competing behaviors: if the competing behavior is 'check phone after pouring coffee,' put the phone in another room during the morning routine.
Test the environment: run through the habit once. Time it. Note anything that slowed you down or required a decision. Eliminate those obstacles.

steps.description: Track your streak (consecutive days of completing the stack) and scale the habit once the stack is automatic.

outputs.name: streak-log
outputs.desc: Daily check: did you complete the stack today? Running streak count. The target is 21 consecutive days before scaling.

outputs.name: scaling-plan
outputs.desc: How to expand the habit once the stack is automatic: from 2 minutes to 5, then 10, then the target duration

process: Track with a simple yes/no daily check. The goal is an unbroken streak. If you miss a day, restart the streak counter. Never miss two days in a row.
The first 21 days are about consistency, not duration. Keep the habit tiny (2 minutes). The habit stack needs to become automatic before you scale.
After 21 consecutive days, increase by 2 minutes. Run another 7 days at the new duration. If the streak holds, increase again.
If scaling breaks the streak, drop back to the previous duration. The habit stack must remain effortless enough that you never skip it.

description: Detect burnout before it becomes clinical by tracking the three dimensions: emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and reduced personal accomplishment. Then design a recovery protocol targeted to the dominant dimension.

steps.description: Assess your current state on the three burnout dimensions: are you emotionally exhausted, cynical/detached, or feeling ineffective?

inputs.name: current-state
inputs.desc: How you are feeling: energy level, attitude toward work, sense of accomplishment

inputs.name: recent-changes
inputs.desc: What changed recently: workload, relationships, role, expectations

outputs.name: exhaustion-score
outputs.desc: Emotional exhaustion assessment (1-10): drained, unable to face the day, feeling like every task takes disproportionate effort

outputs.name: detachment-score
outputs.desc: Depersonalization assessment (1-10): cynicism, treating people as objects, not caring about outcomes

outputs.name: inefficacy-score
outputs.desc: Reduced accomplishment assessment (1-10): feeling that nothing you do matters, that your work has no impact, that you are not good at your job

process: Score emotional exhaustion (1-10): Do you dread going to work? Does every task feel harder than it should? Do you feel drained by the end of the day even if the day was objectively easy? High scores indicate the energy well is empty.

Score depersonalization (1-10): Do you feel cynical about your work or the people you work with? Do you catch yourself not caring about outcomes that used to matter? Are you going through the motions? High scores indicate emotional disconnection.

Score reduced accomplishment (1-10): Do you feel like your work does not matter? That you are not making a difference? That you are failing even when the evidence says otherwise? High scores indicate a meaning deficit.
The dominant dimension determines the recovery approach: exhaustion needs rest and boundary-setting. Detachment needs reconnection and purpose. Inefficacy needs wins and recognition.

steps.description: Identify the specific causes: which aspects of your work or life are driving each dimension.

outputs.name: exhaustion-causes
outputs.desc: Specific causes: overwork, insufficient recovery, emotional labor, unclear boundaries, chronic stress

outputs.name: detachment-causes
outputs.desc: Specific causes: values mismatch, toxic environment, meaningless tasks, lack of autonomy

outputs.name: inefficacy-causes
outputs.desc: Specific causes: no feedback, moving goalposts, perfectionism, imposter syndrome, genuinely poor fit

process: For exhaustion: list everything that drains energy. Not just work tasks, but emotional labor, commute, caregiving, financial stress. Burnout is not just from work; it is from total demand exceeding total capacity.

For detachment: identify what you used to care about that you no longer do. The delta reveals the cause. If you used to care about the team's success and now feel indifferent, something changed in the team or in how your contribution is valued.

For inefficacy: separate fact from feeling. Are you actually ineffective (performance data is poor), or do you feel ineffective despite evidence to the contrary (imposter syndrome)? The solutions are different.

The causes often cluster: overwork (exhaustion) leads to cynicism (detachment) which leads to feeling like nothing matters (inefficacy). Addressing the upstream cause (overwork) often resolves the downstream effects.

steps.description: Design a recovery protocol targeted to your dominant dimension and root causes.

inputs.name: inefficacy-causes
inputs.desc: What is making you feel ineffective

outputs.name: recovery-plan
outputs.desc: Specific daily and weekly actions for recovery: what to add (rest, boundaries, meaning, wins) and what to remove (overcommitments, energy drains, toxic interactions)

outputs.name: boundary-changes
outputs.desc: Boundaries to set: work hours, email access, meeting limits, project load

process: For exhaustion: the primary intervention is reducing demand and increasing recovery. Set hard work hours and enforce them. Take one full day off per week with zero work. Sleep 8 hours. Cancel non-essential commitments for 30 days.

For detachment: the primary intervention is reconnecting with purpose. Schedule 1:1 conversations with people your work helps. Revisit why you chose this work. If the values mismatch is real (not just burnout-colored), begin exploring alternatives.

For inefficacy: the primary intervention is stacking small wins. Choose 3 tasks you can complete this week. Complete them. Celebrate them. Ask a trusted colleague for honest feedback on your recent work. Often, the feeling of inefficacy is disconnected from actual performance.
The 30-day recovery protocol: Week 1 = emergency stabilization (sleep, boundaries, cancel commitments). Week 2-3 = targeted intervention (based on dominant dimension). Week 4 = reassessment.

steps.description: Build a prevention system: monthly self-check, energy boundaries, and early warning signals.

outputs.name: monthly-check-protocol
outputs.desc: A monthly 5-minute self-assessment: rate exhaustion, detachment, and inefficacy. If any score rises above 6, trigger the recovery protocol immediately.

outputs.name: early-warning-signals
outputs.desc: Your personal early warning signs: specific behaviors or feelings that indicate burnout is approaching (e.g., dreading Sunday evenings, snapping at colleagues, abandoning hobbies)

process: Set a monthly calendar reminder for the 3-dimension self-check. Score exhaustion, detachment, and inefficacy 1-10. If any score rises above 6, activate recovery interventions immediately. Do not wait until it reaches 9.

Identify your personal early warning signs. Everyone has them: for some it is dreading Sunday evenings, for others it is snapping at loved ones, for others it is abandoning hobbies. Know your signals.

Build structural prevention: do not overcommit in the first place. Before saying yes to a new commitment, ask: 'What will I stop doing to make room for this?' If the answer is nothing, you are adding demand without reducing load.
Recovery is not a one-time event. It is a recurring need. Schedule recovery proactively (quarterly vacations, weekly off-days, daily downtime) instead of reactively (only resting when you collapse).

description: Build a sustainable movement habit by starting with the minimum effective dose: 20 minutes of walking, 3 times per week. Not a workout plan. A movement plan that you will actually maintain for years.

steps.description: Honestly assess your current movement level: how much do you move, what do you enjoy, and what has failed before.

inputs.name: current-activity
inputs.desc: How much you currently move: exercise, walking, stairs, active hobbies

inputs.name: past-attempts
inputs.desc: Exercise programs you have tried and abandoned, and why they failed

outputs.name: movement-baseline
outputs.desc: Current weekly movement: hours, types, and frequency

outputs.name: failure-patterns
outputs.desc: Why past exercise attempts failed: too ambitious, too boring, too time-consuming, injury, schedule conflict

process: Be honest about the baseline. If you walk 10 minutes a day and nothing else, that is the baseline. Overstating the baseline leads to an overambitious plan that fails.

Review past failures. The most common reasons exercise programs fail: started too aggressively (went from zero to 5 days/week), chose an activity you do not enjoy, required too much time, or required special equipment or location.
Identify what you do enjoy. Walking, swimming, cycling, dancing, sports, yoga. If the activity is not enjoyable, the habit will not survive. Discipline is a finite resource; enjoyment is not.
The goal is not fitness. The goal is a movement habit that you will still be doing in 5 years. This changes the design criteria entirely.

steps.description: Design the minimum effective dose: the least amount of movement that produces measurable health benefits and is easy enough to never skip.

outputs.name: movement-prescription
outputs.desc: The minimum plan: activity type, duration (start at 20 minutes), frequency (3x per week), and intensity (conversational pace)

outputs.name: non-negotiable-minimum
outputs.desc: The absolute floor: even on the worst day, you do this (e.g., a 10-minute walk). Never zero.

process: Start with 20 minutes of walking, 3 times per week. This is enough to produce measurable health benefits (cardiovascular, mood, metabolic) and is easy enough that almost no one will skip it.

Choose an activity you already know you enjoy. If you hate running, do not prescribe running. If you like walking, walk. If you like swimming, swim. Enjoyment is the strongest predictor of long-term adherence.
Set a non-negotiable minimum: even on the worst day, you do something. A 10-minute walk counts. Zero does not. The habit of movement matters more than the intensity of any single session.
No gym membership required. The research shows that walking produces 80% of the health benefits of intense exercise. The barrier to entry must be as low as possible.

steps.description: Schedule movement at specific times with specific triggers so it becomes automatic.

outputs.name: movement-schedule
outputs.desc: Specific days and times: 'Monday, Wednesday, Friday at 7am: 20-minute walk from my front door'

outputs.name: trigger-setup
outputs.desc: The trigger that initiates movement: alarm, habit stack, calendar event, or environmental cue (e.g., shoes by the door)

process: Schedule specific days and times. 'I will exercise this week' fails. 'Monday, Wednesday, Friday at 7am' succeeds. Specificity turns intention into behavior.
Use a habit stack if possible: 'After I finish my morning coffee, I walk for 20 minutes.' The coffee habit triggers the movement habit.
Prepare the environment: shoes and clothes laid out the night before. If you have to search for shoes at 7am, you will skip it.
Protect the time: treat movement like a meeting. It goes on the calendar. It is not the first thing cancelled when the day gets busy.

steps.description: After 30 days of consistency, expand gradually: longer duration, higher intensity, or additional days. Never more than one variable at a time.

outputs.name: expansion-plan
outputs.desc: Month 2: increase duration to 30 minutes. Month 3: add a 4th day. Month 4: increase intensity on one day. Never more than one change per month.

outputs.name: plateau-response
outputs.desc: If progress stalls or motivation drops, return to the minimum effective dose rather than quitting entirely

process: Change one variable per month: duration OR frequency OR intensity. Never two at once. Two simultaneous changes double the failure risk.
Month 2: increase from 20 to 30 minutes. Month 3: add a 4th day. Month 4: increase intensity on one session (hills, intervals, or faster pace). This slow progression builds a stable habit.
If you miss a week, do not 'make up for it' by doubling the next week. Return to the minimum dose and rebuild the streak.

The long-term target is 150 minutes of moderate activity per week (the WHO recommendation). At the progression rate above, you reach it in month 4. Most people who start at 150 minutes quit in month 1.

description: Build a stress response protocol: detect stress signals early, interrupt the cortisol cascade with a 90-second intervention, and design your day to prevent chronic stress accumulation.

steps.description: Identify your personal stress signals: the physical and behavioral signs that appear before you consciously feel stressed.

inputs.name: stress-history
inputs.desc: Times when you have been highly stressed: what triggered it, how it felt, what you did

inputs.name: current-stress-level
inputs.desc: Your current stress level and what is driving it

outputs.name: physical-signals
outputs.desc: Your body's stress signals: jaw clenching, shoulder tension, shallow breathing, stomach tightness, headache, racing heart

outputs.name: behavioral-signals
outputs.desc: Your behavioral stress signals: snapping at people, checking phone compulsively, eating for comfort, procrastinating, difficulty sleeping

process: Think about the last 3 times you were highly stressed. Before you consciously realized you were stressed, what was your body doing? Jaw clenched? Shoulders up? Breathing shallow?
Identify your behavioral tells. Stress shows in behavior before it shows in conscious awareness. Some people eat. Some withdraw. Some get irritable. Some clean obsessively. Know your pattern.
Create a short checklist of your top 3 physical and top 3 behavioral signals. Check this list twice daily (morning and afternoon) to catch stress early.
Early detection is the key: a cortisol spike that is interrupted in the first 90 seconds dissipates quickly. A cortisol spike that runs for hours becomes chronic stress.

steps.description: Design a 90-second intervention that interrupts the stress response: physiological sigh, box breathing, or cold water on the face.

outputs.name: intervention-menu
outputs.desc: 3 interventions that work in 90 seconds: physiological sigh (double inhale, long exhale), box breathing (4-4-4-4), and cold exposure (cold water on wrists or face)

outputs.name: context-matching
outputs.desc: Which intervention to use in which context: sigh at desk, box breathing in a meeting, cold water in a bathroom

process: The physiological sigh is the fastest intervention: two quick inhales through the nose, then one long exhale through the mouth. This activates the parasympathetic nervous system within seconds.
Box breathing for sustained calm: inhale 4 seconds, hold 4 seconds, exhale 4 seconds, hold 4 seconds. Repeat 3-4 cycles. This takes 60-90 seconds and is invisible in a meeting.
Cold exposure: run cold water over your wrists for 30 seconds, or splash cold water on your face. This triggers the dive reflex, which slows heart rate and calms the nervous system.
Practice the interventions when you are NOT stressed. The habit must be automatic so that when a stress signal fires, the intervention launches without deliberation.

steps.description: Design your day to prevent chronic stress accumulation: scheduled recovery, transition rituals, and a hard stop.

outputs.name: prevention-schedule
outputs.desc: Daily recovery touchpoints: morning grounding (5 min), mid-day movement (10 min), end-of-day shutdown ritual (10 min)

outputs.name: hard-stop-protocol
outputs.desc: A defined end-of-work time with a shutdown ritual that signals to the brain that work is done

process: Morning grounding: 5 minutes of intentional calm before opening email or starting work. This sets the baseline for the day. Starting the day in a reactive state (email, news) starts the cortisol early.
Mid-day movement: a 10-minute walk between the morning and afternoon blocks. Movement metabolizes cortisol. A sedentary person accumulates cortisol; a moving person processes it.
End-of-day shutdown: at a defined time, write tomorrow's top 3 tasks, close all tabs, and say 'Shutdown complete' (or your own phrase). This ritual tells the brain to stop processing work.

The hard stop is not optional on most days. Working until you fall asleep means cortisol is still elevated during sleep, which degrades sleep quality, which increases stress the next day. The cycle must be broken.

steps.description: Monthly assessment: is your baseline stress level rising or falling? If rising, identify the structural cause and change it.

outputs.name: monthly-stress-score
outputs.desc: Monthly average stress rating (1-10) compared to previous months

outputs.name: structural-changes
outputs.desc: If the trend is rising: the specific structural change needed (reduce workload, set boundaries, address relationship conflict, or change environment)

process: Rate your stress 1-10 at the end of each week. Average the 4 weekly scores for a monthly score.
Compare to previous months. A rising trend over 2+ months indicates a structural problem that daily interventions cannot solve. Something needs to change.
Structural changes: if the cause is workload, reduce it. If the cause is a relationship, address it. If the cause is financial, plan for it. If the cause is health, see a professional.
Daily stress management treats symptoms. Monthly assessment treats causes. Both are necessary.

description: Design a sustainable nutrition system, not a diet. A diet is temporary restriction. A system is a set of defaults that you maintain without willpower: what you stock, what you prepare, and what you default to when tired.

steps.description: Audit what you actually eat for 7 days, without changing anything. Most people do not know what they eat.

inputs.name: nutrition-goals
inputs.desc: What you want to change: energy, weight, health markers, performance

outputs.name: food-log
outputs.desc: 7-day log: every meal, snack, and drink with approximate portions and times

outputs.name: eating-patterns
outputs.desc: Patterns: meal timing, snacking frequency, default choices when tired, weekend vs weekday differences

process: Log everything for 7 days without trying to eat differently. The point is to see reality, not to perform good behavior. Include drinks (especially alcohol and sugary drinks).
Note the context of each meal: where were you, what time was it, how hungry were you, and was it planned or improvised? Improvised meals are usually lower quality.
Identify the default choices: what do you eat when you are tired and do not want to cook? What do you reach for as a snack? These defaults determine 80% of your nutrition over a year.
Calculate rough proportions: how much of your food is whole/minimally processed vs ultra-processed? A simple test: if you cannot identify all the ingredients by looking at it, it is processed.

steps.description: Design 5 default meals that you can prepare in under 20 minutes, that you enjoy, and that meet basic nutritional needs. These are your defaults, not your only meals.

outputs.name: default-meals
outputs.desc: 5 go-to meals: 2 breakfasts, 2 dinners, and 1 lunch that you enjoy, can prepare quickly, and meet protein/vegetable targets

outputs.name: grocery-template
outputs.desc: A standard grocery list for these 5 meals that you can reorder weekly with minimal thought

process: Choose 5 meals you already like (or close variations). Do not introduce entirely new foods. Willpower is limited; new foods require willpower. Familiar foods that are slightly healthier require almost none.
Each meal should have protein (palm-sized portion), vegetables (fill half the plate), and a starch or grain. This is not strict macronutrient counting; it is a simple visual template.
Each meal must be preparable in under 20 minutes. Meals that take 45 minutes get skipped for takeout on busy nights. Speed is a feature, not a compromise.
Build a standard grocery list for these 5 meals. Automate the grocery order if possible. Decision fatigue around 'what to eat' is the primary failure mode of nutrition systems.

steps.description: Redesign your food environment: what is visible, accessible, and convenient determines what you eat more than willpower.

outputs.name: environment-changes
outputs.desc: Kitchen and workspace changes: healthy defaults visible and accessible, unhealthy options hidden or removed

outputs.name: snack-defaults
outputs.desc: Default snacks pre-portioned and accessible: nuts, fruit, yogurt, cut vegetables. Replace, do not just remove.

process: Put healthy foods at eye level in the fridge and pantry. Move less healthy options to harder-to-reach locations. Visibility drives consumption more than preference.
Pre-portion snacks. A bag of nuts on the counter leads to eating a handful. A pre-portioned cup of nuts leads to eating a serving. Portion control is an environment problem, not a willpower problem.
Replace, do not remove. Removing snacks without replacing them creates a vacuum that willpower must fill. Replacing chips with nuts creates a new default that requires no willpower.
If you eat at your desk, stock desk snacks that are nutritious. Hungry people eat what is closest. If the closest option is a protein bar instead of a candy bar, you eat better without deciding to.

steps.description: Run the system for 30 days, then iterate. The goal is consistency, not perfection. An 80% hit rate on default meals is excellent.

outputs.name: system-review
outputs.desc: 30-day review: how many days did you use default meals, how do you feel (energy, satiety, digestion), and what meals need adjustment

outputs.name: iteration-changes
outputs.desc: Swap out meals that did not work, adjust portions, add variety to the rotation

process: Track simply: did you eat a default meal today? Yes or no. 80% (24 of 30 days) is excellent. 60% needs troubleshooting. Below 50% means the defaults are not convenient enough or not enjoyable enough.
After 30 days, assess: do you have more energy? Are you less hungry between meals? Are you spending less time deciding what to eat? These are the metrics that matter, not the scale.
Swap out any default meal that you skipped more than twice. It is not sustainable for you. Replace it with something you will actually eat.
Add one new default meal per month. Over 6 months, you build a rotation of 10+ meals. Variety prevents boredom without requiring daily decision-making.

description: Audit your digital habits: screen time, notification frequency, social media consumption, and their effect on focus, sleep, and mood. Then redesign the defaults.

steps.description: Measure your actual digital usage for 7 days: screen time by app, pickup frequency, and notification count.

inputs.name: current-habits
inputs.desc: Your sense of how much you use your phone and computer

inputs.name: concerns
inputs.desc: What prompted this audit: difficulty focusing, poor sleep, anxiety, time lost

outputs.name: usage-data
outputs.desc: 7-day averages: total screen time, top 5 apps by time, phone pickups per day, notification count per day

outputs.name: reality-gap
outputs.desc: The gap between how much you thought you used your devices and how much you actually do (most people underestimate by 50-100%)

process: Use your phone's built-in screen time tracker (iOS Screen Time or Android Digital Wellbeing) for 7 days. Do not change your behavior; observe it.
Record: total screen time per day, top 5 apps by time, number of phone pickups per day, and total notifications per day.
Most people are surprised: average screen time is 3-4 hours per day, average pickups are 80-100 per day, and average notifications are 60-80 per day. Your numbers reveal the magnitude of the problem.
Calculate the cost: if you spend 3 hours per day on your phone, that is 21 hours per week, or 1,095 hours per year. What would you do with 1,000 hours?

steps.description: Audit every notification source and eliminate all except those that require immediate action.

outputs.name: notification-audit
outputs.desc: Every app that sends notifications, categorized: essential (calls, messages from key people), useful (calendar, reminders), and unnecessary (social media, news, marketing)

outputs.name: notification-policy
outputs.desc: New policy: only essential notifications are allowed. Everything else is disabled.

process: List every app that sends notifications. For each, ask: does this notification require me to act in the next hour? If no, disable it.
Essential notifications: calls and texts from family and close colleagues. Calendar reminders. Truly urgent work alerts.
Disable everything else: social media notifications, email notifications, news alerts, app marketing, game notifications. You will check these on your own schedule, not when the app decides.

Notifications are not information; they are interruptions. Every notification breaks your focus and takes 23 minutes to recover from (research on context switching). 60 notifications per day = potentially 23 hours of recovery time.

steps.description: Redesign your phone and computer defaults: home screen, app placement, and access patterns to reduce mindless consumption.

outputs.name: device-redesign
outputs.desc: Home screen with only productivity and communication apps. Social media and entertainment apps moved to a secondary screen or removed entirely.

outputs.name: access-friction
outputs.desc: Friction added to time-sink apps: logged out, app limits set, or browser-only access

process: Home screen: only apps you use for productive purposes (calendar, notes, maps, phone, messages). Remove all social media and entertainment apps from the home screen.

Add friction to time-sink apps: log out after each use (so you must log in each time), set app time limits, or delete the app and access only through the browser (browser versions are deliberately less engaging).

Remove infinite-scroll apps from easy access. The design of these apps is specifically engineered to keep you scrolling. Accessing them should require deliberate effort, not an absent-minded thumb tap.
Set your phone to grayscale in the evenings. Color is a significant driver of engagement. A grayscale phone is functionally useful but visually boring, which reduces mindless pickup.

steps.description: Set digital boundaries: phone-free times, device-free spaces, and a weekly review of usage trends.

outputs.name: digital-boundaries
outputs.desc: Specific rules: no phone in bedroom, no phone during meals, no phone for the first 30 minutes after waking, no phone after 9pm

outputs.name: weekly-review
outputs.desc: A weekly 5-minute check: screen time this week vs last week, pickups this week vs last week, and subjective focus/mood assessment

process: Set phone-free zones: bedroom (improves sleep), dining table (improves relationships), and first 30 minutes after waking (reduces reactive state).
Set phone-free times: after 9pm (or 2 hours before bed), during focused work blocks, and during face-to-face conversations.
Weekly review: check screen time vs previous week. Is the trend down? Check pickups. Check which apps consumed the most time. Adjust access friction for any app that is creeping up.
The goal is not zero screen time. Digital tools are useful. The goal is intentional use: you choose when to engage instead of the app choosing for you.
